analysis.one_liner: Takes military sexual assault prosecutions out of the chain of command and puts them under independent civilian oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 159 House cosponsors but never received a vote; it died in the House Armed Services Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The STOP Act would have created a civilian-led council inside the Pentagon and an independent office to handle reports of sexual assault, so that reports no longer pass through the soldier's own commanders. It would have created a Director of Military Prosecutions with sole authority to send sexual assault cases to court-martial, replacing the current system in which a commander decides whether a case goes forward. The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and never received a markup or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members who are sexually assaulted, especially those whose assailant is in their own chain of command. The bill's findings cite a Pentagon survey finding that about 19,000 incidents occurred in 2010 and that 86% went unreported, a rate the bill attributes to having to report through the same command structure that may include the offender or the offender's superiors. It would also benefit victims' advocates and military prosecutors by giving an independent office, not commanders, control over whether cases are prosecuted.

how_it_helps.text: Requires protocols ensuring every sexual assault report goes directly to an independent Sexual Assault Oversight and Response Office rather than through the chain of command.

Creates a Director of Military Prosecutions, appointed by a civilian-majority council, with 'independent and final authority' to prosecute all sexual-related offenses and refer them to courts-martial, replacing the commander's power to decide whether a case proceeds.

Establishes a Sexual Assault Oversight and Response Council composed mostly of civilians and independent from the military chain of command, to oversee investigations, victim protections, training, and prosecutions.
Requires the Inspector General to review a statistically significant sample of sexual assault cases quarterly, and requires an annual report to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Military commanders lose their authority to decide whether sexual assault cases in their units go to court-martial, a power they have held under the military justice system since its founding. The Pentagon would bear the cost of standing up a new office, transferring the existing Sexual Assault Prevention and Response Office into it, and running quarterly Inspector General case reviews. Good-faith opponents also argued that separating commanders from prosecution weakens the accountability structure on which military order depends.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes prosecutorial discretion from unit commanders entirely; defenders of the traditional system argued that commanders bear responsibility for their units' readiness and discipline, and that an independent prosecutor insulated from command could weaken that accountability structure.

The bill creates a new standing bureaucracy — a council, an office with an executive director, a director of prosecutions, and quarterly Inspector General reviews — and the bill does not specify how its budget is funded.
Concentrating all sexual assault charging decisions in one appointed Director could create its own bottleneck for the thousands of cases the bill's findings say occur each year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real and was the center of the 2013 debate: removing commanders from prosecution decisions directly addresses the conflict of interest the bill itself identifies — a commander may control the careers of both victim and offender — but it also strips commanders of a traditional discipline tool and adds a new layer of bureaucracy. On the findings in the bill itself, with 86% of assaults unreported and the adjudication system lacking independence, the case that the existing system was failing victims is strong, and the cost of the reform falls mainly on the institution the bill seeks to check.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and then to its Military Personnel subcommittee, and never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jackie Speier introduced the bill on April 17, 2013, with an unusually large group of original cosponsors named in the bill itself.
The bill attracted 159 cosponsors — 158 Democrats and 1 Republican — which would have been more than a third of the House if all had voted yes.

The House referred the bill to the Armed Services Committee on the day of introduction, and on May 6, 2013 it was referred to the subcommittee on Military Personnel; no further action was ever taken on the bill.

The bill's findings cited a Department of Defense survey showing only 13.5% of service members reported sexual assaults, meaning an estimated 19,000-plus incidents occurred in 2010, with 86% unreported, and stated that command discretion over whether cases go to court-martial raises concerns about conflicts of interest and abuse of power.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The military chain of command is better off: commanders kept their authority to decide whether sexual assault cases in their units are prosecuted, and the independent civilian council and prosecutor the bill would have created never came into existence. Members of the Armed Services Committee also faced no vote on a reform that had 159 cosponsors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Military commanders and House committee leadership

for.name: Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the STOP Act and assembled 158 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsors.

for.name: Walter Jones
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican to do so.

against.name: Howard McKeon
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or brought the bill to a vote; the bill sat in committee and subcommittee for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to the Military Personnel subcommittee on May 6, 2013; took no further action recorded in the bill's history.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 158 of the 159 cosponsors were Democrats, with Representative Walter Jones of North Carolina the sole Republican — and the committee that buried the bill was chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Military chain of command (senior commanders and convening authorities)
industries.note: The bill strips commanders of the power to decide whether sexual assault cases in their own units go to court-martial, transferring that authority to an independent civilian-appointed prosecutor. Commanders' discretion is the mechanism the bill targets as the source of underreporting and conflicted decisions.

The Pentagon would have gained a new office, council, and director, but would lose control over how sexual assault reports and prosecutions are handled, with oversight shifting to civilians independent of the chain of command and quarterly Inspector General reviews imposed.
